slides.headline: Swimmer? Your shoulders will like this
slides.sub: How clinical Pilates can support your time in the pool.

slides.title: Swimming favours some muscles
slides.body: Freestyle leans heavily on the chest and the front of the shoulder. Pilates can balance that with upper back and shoulder blade work that swimming doesn't always train.

slides.title: Shoulder blade control
slides.body: Reformer arm work, rows and slow wall slides help the shoulder blade move smoothly as your arm reaches overhead, which can make long sets feel more comfortable.

slides.title: A steady trunk, a longer line
slides.body: Side planks, dead bugs and controlled leg work train you to hold a long, steady body position. That can reduce the sway that lets your legs sink in the water.

slides.title: Rotation for easier breathing
slides.body: Upper back rotation exercises can make turning to breathe feel easier, so your neck and lower back don't have to do all the twisting on every stroke.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Shoulder pain that wakes you at night, painful clicking, weakness lifting your arm, or pain lasting more than a couple of weeks deserves an assessment before you add more laps.

slides.headline: Stronger strokes start on land
slides.body: Our Pilates team at Hybrid Physiotherapy assesses how you move, then builds a program around your swimming. Book online via the link in bio.

caption:
Swimmer? Your shoulders might appreciate some time on land. 🏊

Freestyle relies heavily on the chest and front of the shoulder. Clinical Pilates can balance that with shoulder blade control, upper back strength and rotation work, plus a steady trunk that helps you hold a long line in the water.

Many swimmers find one or two sessions a week fits nicely around pool training. Shoulder pain that wakes you at night, weakness lifting your arm or pain lasting more than a couple of weeks is worth getting assessed before adding more laps.
